imageAlt: How to Raise Funds for Startup Business in India: 2026 Guide
takeaways: Angel investors in India work under the SEBI AIF (Alternate Investment Fund) Category I framework. Major networks include the Indian Angel Network, LetsVenture, Mumbai Angels, and AngelList India. Typical tickets run from ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore for 5–20% equity at seed.

Venture Capital funds are SEBI-registered AIFs — Category I (VCFs) for early-stage and Category II (PE/growth funds) for later stages. Most VC funds set a minimum of ₹5 crore and usually want at least ₹1–5 crore in annualised revenue or strong user traction.

DPIIT recognition is a useful credibility marker for both angels and VCs — it signals regulatory compliance, access to government co-investment schemes, and verified startup status under the DPIIT definition.

blocks.text: India now hosts the world's third-largest startup ecosystem, with more than 1.1 lakh DPIIT-recognised startups as of 2026. Across every stage, founders still hit the same bottleneck: finding capital that arrives at the right moment and on terms they can live with.

Knowing how to raise funds for a startup in India is basic operating knowledge, not a nice-to-have. The market has grown up: non-dilutive government programmes, SEBI-regulated angel networks, RBI-supervised debt products, and private venture capital are all open to founders who understand the process and meet compliance tests.

This guide lays out the main funding paths available in India in 2026 — government grants and collateral-free loans as well as angel investment and venture capital — together with eligibility, paperwork, and a step-by-step application path for each.
What is Startup Funding?

Startup funding is money a business uses to pay costs it cannot yet cover from its own sales. It generally comes in two shapes: dilutive funding (equity given for capital — angel rounds, venture capital) and non-dilutive funding (no equity given — government grants, subsidies, and collateral-free loans).

Which mix you choose depends on stage, sector, revenue traction, and how much ownership you want to keep. For most Indian startups, the sounder sequence is to take non-dilutive money first — government grants and [government-backed MSME loan schemes](/scheme) — so runway stretches before any dilutive round. That leaves more founder equity for later stages, when valuations are typically much higher.
Funding Routes at a Glance
Four broad buckets make up India's startup funding system. Each sits under a different regulator and fits a different stage of the business:
Government Grants & Schemes

Grants are funds that central and state governments pay out and do not ask back, meant to back startups and MSMEs. More than 60 central-government schemes are live in 2026, yet under 8% of eligible firms actually receive them — mainly because paperwork is incomplete and many businesses never hear of the scheme. If the mechanics are unfamiliar, read [how government grants actually work](/blogs/how-government-grants-work) before you shortlist programmes.
These are the central-government schemes that matter most for startups and MSMEs in 2026:

items.title: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS)
items.body: Offers up to ₹20 lakh as a non-repayable grant for proof-of-concept and prototype work, plus up to ₹50 lakh as convertible debt for market entry and commercialisation. Only DPIIT-recognised startups can apply, and only through DPIIT-approved incubators. File at seedfund.startupindia.gov.in, and study [the scheme's full eligibility and application flow](/scheme/seed-fund) before you approach an incubator.

items.title: PMEGP (Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme)
items.body: Gives a 25–35% capital subsidy on project costs up to ₹50 lakh for manufacturing units and ₹20 lakh for service enterprises. Open to new micro enterprises outside farming. File through kviconline.gov.in via District Industries Centres or KVIC/KVIB offices.

items.title: Stand-Up India Scheme
items.body: Offers composite loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore at subsidised interest, reserved for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs starting greenfield manufacturing, services, or trading units. Scheduled commercial banks run the scheme — the [Stand-Up India loan terms](/scheme/standup) describe the margin money and repayment structure banks use.

items.title: Atal Innovation Mission (AIM)
items.body: NITI Aayog's main innovation programme backs startups through Atal Incubation Centres (AICs) and Atal New India Challenges. It supplies incubation grants, mentoring, and market linkages for deep-tech, social-impact, and sector-focused startups.

items.title: ASPIRE (A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries and Entrepreneurship)
items.body: Offers incubation and seed money to rural and agri-based startups via NABARD-linked Livelihood Business Incubators (LBIs) and Technology Business Incubators (TBIs). Aimed at startups with a rural, agri-processing, or social-sector focus.

blocks.text: Collateral-Free Loan Schemes
Where a startup or MSME has no fixed assets to pledge, government-backed credit guarantees let banks lend without asking for collateral.

items.title: CGTMSE (Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro & Small Enterprises)
items.body: Allows collateral-free and third-party-guarantee-free loans up to ₹5 crore from any scheduled commercial bank, SIDBI, or NBFC-MFI. The Trust gives the lender a 75–85% credit guarantee, which removes the collateral hurdle. Udyam registration is compulsory. This is the scheme most MSMEs use for working capital and term loans — see how the [credit guarantee cover for micro and small enterprises](/scheme/cgtmse) is priced and claimed.

items.title: Mudra Yojana (PMMY)
items.body: Lends in three bands: Shishu (up to ₹50,000 for micro enterprises), Kishore (₹50,000–₹5 lakh for established small businesses), and Tarun (₹5 lakh–₹20 lakh for growth-stage businesses). Available at all PSU banks, private banks, RRBs, and MFIs. No collateral is required at any [Mudra loan tier](/scheme/mudra).

items.title: PSB Loans in 59 Minutes
items.body: An RBI-backed digital platform (psbloansin59minutes.com) that issues in-principle approval for MSME loans up to ₹5 crore within one hour, using GST returns, ITR data, and bank-statement analysis. Final disbursement typically drops from weeks to 7–10 working days.

items.title: SIDBI Direct Finance
items.body: SIDBI's direct-lending window offers growth-stage MSMEs term loans and working capital from ₹10 lakh to ₹25 crore at competitive rates, with flexible collateral norms for DPIIT-recognised startups and tech-enabled businesses.

blocks.text: Angel Investment & Venture Capital

Equity funding means selling a slice of the company for capital. It fits growth or scale stages — after non-dilutive options have been used — once you can show traction, product-market fit, or defensible IP. Convertible notes, SAFEs and priced rounds dilute in different ways, so map [which funding instrument fits your stage](/services/startup) before you open a round.

items: Angel investors in India work under the SEBI AIF (Alternate Investment Fund) Category I framework. Major networks include the Indian Angel Network, LetsVenture, Mumbai Angels, and AngelList India. Typical tickets run from ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore for 5–20% equity at seed.

Venture Capital funds are SEBI-registered AIFs — Category I (VCFs) for early-stage and Category II (PE/growth funds) for later stages. Most VC funds set a minimum of ₹5 crore and usually want at least ₹1–5 crore in annualised revenue or strong user traction.

DPIIT recognition is a useful credibility marker for both angels and VCs — it signals regulatory compliance, access to government co-investment schemes, and verified startup status under the DPIIT definition.

Prerequisites for institutional equity fundraising: a clean cap table, current MCA annual filings, CA-certified audited financials, no outstanding regulatory dues (GST, TDS, PF/ESI), and a prepared investor pitch deck with 3-year financial projections.
Do not overvalue at seed. A seed valuation above ₹10–15 crore without real traction or defensible IP raises down-round risk at Series A and weakens follow-on appetite.

blocks.text: Eligibility Criteria at a Glance
Rules differ by scheme and route, but these requirements show up across most central-government and institutional programmes in 2026:

items: DPIIT recognition certificate — mandatory for SISFS, AIM grants, Stand-Up India benefits, and most Startup India linked state schemes
Udyam registration — mandatory for CGTMSE, Mudra Tarun, PMEGP, and most MSME bank loan and subsidy schemes
Incorporated as Private Limited Company, LLP, One Person Company, or registered Partnership Firm
GST registration — required for most schemes with a project cost or loan requirement above ₹20 lakh
PAN card and active current account in the business's name
Promoter-director CIBIL score of 700 or above (for all bank loan and NBFC schemes)
No wilful default or NPA classification with any bank, NBFC, or financial institution at the time of application
ITR filed for at least 1 financial year (2 years preferred for loan applications above ₹25 lakh)
MCA annual filings current — ROC return defaults are a common and automatic rejection trigger for company applicants

blocks.text: Documents Required for Startup Funding

Assemble this pack before you approach a government scheme, a bank, or an investor. Ready, certified papers typically cut approval time by 40–60%. The list almost fully overlaps with the [legal paperwork every startup should keep current](/blogs/startup-legal-documents), so one compilation serves both needs.

items: PAN card and Aadhaar of all directors / promoters / partners
DPIIT recognition certificate (apply free at startupindia.gov.in — required before applying to any government startup scheme)
Udyam registration certificate (apply free at udyamregistration.gov.in — required for all MSME schemes)
GST registration certificate (GSTIN) and last 12 months GST returns
Certificate of Incorporation + MOA & AOA (for Private Limited / OPC) or LLP Agreement (for LLP) or Partnership Deed
Last 2 years CA-certified audited financial statements — Profit & Loss, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement
Last 12 months bank statements for all business accounts
Detailed Project Report (DPR) or Business Plan covering market opportunity, fund utilisation plan, and 3-year financial projections
Pitch deck (required for SISFS incubator applications, angel networks, and VC funds)
Latest ITR acknowledgement for the company and all promoter-directors
Shareholding / cap table document signed by all shareholders
No-dues certificate from existing lenders (if any outstanding loans)

blocks.text: Step-by-Step: How to Apply for Startup Funding
Use this eight-step sequence to move from a funding need to money in the bank without wasted cycles:

items.title: Assess your stage and funding need
items.body: Match your stage — ideation, proof-of-concept, prototype, early revenue, or scale — to the right funding path. Non-dilutive grants suit early stages; equity makes more sense at scale, when valuations are higher and each rupee raised costs less ownership.

items.title: Obtain DPIIT recognition
items.body: Apply free at startupindia.gov.in. Recognition is typically granted within 2–3 working days and is a mandatory prerequisite for SISFS, Atal Innovation Mission grants, Stand-Up India, and most state startup schemes. If the write-up or supporting documents are holding you back, Vikas Bharat handles [Startup India recognition and certification](/services/startup) end to end.

items.title: Register on Udyam (if MSME-eligible)
items.body: If your business falls within MSME turnover thresholds (up to ₹250 crore for medium enterprises), register free at udyamregistration.gov.in. Required for CGTMSE, Mudra, PMEGP, and all bank MSME loan schemes. Businesses that are not yet incorporated should settle [company and Udyam registration](/services/registration) first, since the entity details flow into every later application.

items.title: Prepare your documentation pack
items.body: Compile all documents from the list above. Have your Chartered Accountant certify financial statements before applying. Incomplete or uncertified documents are the single most common cause of government scheme rejections.

items.title: Select the right scheme and portal
items.body: SISFS → apply through a DPIIT-approved incubator at seedfund.startupindia.gov.in. PMEGP → kviconline.gov.in. Mudra → your bank branch directly. CGTMSE → apply for an MSME loan at any scheduled commercial bank and request CGTMSE coverage. VC → approach SEBI-registered AIF fund managers via warm introductions or platforms like LetsVenture.

items.title: Submit your application accurately
items.body: Fill all online form fields carefully — errors in company name spelling, PAN, or Udyam number are grounds for automatic rejection. Upload documents in the portal's required format (typically PDF, under 2 MB each).

items.title: Track your application and respond promptly
items.body: Monitor your application status on the scheme portal. Respond to any query or clarification request within 48 hours. Delayed responses are treated as non-responsiveness and routinely result in rejection without the option to reapply in the same cycle.

items.title: Post-sanction compliance
items.body: After funds are disbursed, maintain utilisation certificates (UCs), submit quarterly and annual progress reports as required, and comply with all audit requirements stated in the sanction letter. Non-compliance can trigger fund recovery action and may blacklist your business from future central and state government schemes.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes That Kill Applications
These errors most often lead to scheme rejections, loan refusals, and investor pass-overs:

items: Applying without DPIIT recognition — it is a hard prerequisite for most central government startup schemes and cannot be bypassed
Submitting uncertified or outdated financials — all financial statements must be CA-certified and within the current or immediately preceding assessment year
Fund utilisation plan mismatched with the scheme's eligible expenditure list — read the scheme guidelines in full before drafting your DPR; ineligible expenditure heads are flagged immediately
MCA annual return defaults — ROC filing arrears trigger automatic red flags for government evaluators and institutional investors; clear all defaults before applying
Overvaluing at the seed stage — inflated seed valuations compress future fundraising options and signal poor financial judgment to Series A investors
Applying for sector-restricted schemes outside your eligible sector — many central and state schemes have hard sector-specific criteria; verify before applying to avoid wasted processing time
Low or unchecked promoter CIBIL score — even a single EMI default on a promoter-director's personal credit report is sufficient to disqualify a CGTMSE or Mudra Tarun loan application

Overlooking state-level schemes — Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu operate high-value [startup grant and subsidy programmes](/scheme) that are significantly under-applied to by eligible businesses

Conclusion

Raising startup capital in India in 2026 is a structured process, not a privilege limited to well-connected founders. DPIIT's recognition programme, SIDBI's collateral-free lending, and a maturing private equity market have opened capital across sectors and regions.

Preparation is the real differentiator: lock in compliance credentials early (DPIIT recognition, Udyam, GST), keep certified financials current, and pick the funding path that matches your stage and business type. Whether the target is a ₹10 lakh seed grant or a ₹5 crore Series A, the sequence does not change — know the options, prepare the papers, and file accurately.

blocks.text: Why Government Grants Matter for MSMEs

Grants are funds that central and state governments pay out and never ask back, intended to help MSMEs and startups. Unlike a loan, a grant carries no repayment, which makes it one of the most useful ways to finance an early-stage or expanding firm.

More than 60 central-government schemes currently target MSMEs across manufacturing, technology, agri-processing, handicrafts and other sectors. Yet fewer than 8% of eligible MSMEs actually receive the money, mainly because owners do not know the programmes exist and because paperwork is incomplete.

The practical upside: most grants accept applications on a rolling basis, and filing is fully online. If the business is registered and the documents are in order, there is little reason to leave this capital unused.

blocks.text: Central Grant Schemes — Detailed Breakdown
These are the central-government grant programmes that matter most for MSMEs and startups in 2026, with the detail you need to decide where to apply:

items.title: PMEGP (Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme)
items.body: Pays a 25–35% capital subsidy on project cost for new manufacturing units (project up to ₹50 lakh) and service enterprises (project up to ₹20 lakh). SC/ST, women, ex-servicemen, and rural units receive a higher subsidy. File through kviconline.gov.in via your District Industries Centre (DIC) or KVIC office. This remains one of the most used programmes for first-time entrepreneurs.

items.title: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS)
items.body: Pays up to ₹20 lakh as a non-repayable grant for proof-of-concept and prototype work, and up to ₹50 lakh as convertible debt for market entry and scaling. Limited to DPIIT-recognised startups (incorporated under 10 years, turnover below ₹100 crore). Applications go through DPIIT-approved incubators at seedfund.startupindia.gov.in — not straight to DPIIT.

items.title: Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS)
items.body: Gives a 15% upfront capital subsidy (capped at ₹15 lakh) to small-scale industries upgrading plant, machinery or technology. Open to units in 51 approved sub-sectors. The linked loan must come from a scheduled commercial bank — the subsidy is credited to that loan account. Best for existing manufacturers modernising equipment.

items.title: ASPIRE (A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries and Entrepreneurship)
items.body: Backs agri-based startups and rural entrepreneurs with incubation grants and seed money through NABARD-linked Livelihood Business Incubators (LBIs) and Technology Business Incubators (TBIs). Especially relevant for food processing, dairy, handicrafts, and rural service units.

items.title: NSIC Marketing Assistance Scheme
items.body: Refunds marketing and trade-fair costs for MSMEs that take part in domestic and international exhibitions. Stall charges, freight, and promotional material are covered. Registered Udyam MSMEs apply on NSIC’s online portal. A low-effort programme worth filing if you attend trade events.

blocks.text: More Central Schemes Worth Knowing
Three further central programmes are often skipped, yet they matter for agri, deep-tech, and underrepresented founder groups:

items.title: RKVY-RAFTAAR (Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana — Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and Allied sector Rejuvenation)
items.body: A large agri-focused grant run by the Ministry of Agriculture. Pays up to ₹5 lakh at ideation and up to ₹25 lakh for product development and market entry. Agri-tech startups, food-processing firms, and rural agri entrepreneurs are the main users. Applications run through RKVY-RAFTAAR Agri-Business Incubators (R-ABIs) nationwide.

items.title: Nidhi Prayas (Promoting and Accelerating Young and Aspiring Innovators and Startups)
items.body: A Department of Science and Technology (DST) programme that pays up to ₹10 lakh to individual innovators and early-stage startups for hardware and deep-tech prototype work. Best for engineering and technology startups that already have a working proof-of-concept. Run through DST-supported incubators.

items.title: Stand-Up India Scheme
items.body: Offers composite term loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore at competitive rates to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs starting greenfield manufacturing, services, or trading units. Built for first-generation entrepreneurs from underrepresented groups. File through scheduled commercial banks; standupmitra.in offers guidance.

blocks.text: State-Level Grant Schemes

Each Indian state also runs its own MSME grant and subsidy programmes. These are often less crowded than central schemes simply because fewer firms know they exist. Check these programmes in five major states:

items.title: Gujarat — i Create and GUJCOAST
items.body: Gujarat’s iCreate (International Centre for Entrepreneurship and Technology) supports tech and social-impact startups with seed grants up to ₹10 lakh plus incubation. The Gujarat Council of Science and Technology (GUJCOST) adds grants for science-based startups and research commercialisation.

items.title: Karnataka — Elevate 100 and Karnataka Startup Cell
items.body: Elevate 100, from Karnataka’s Department of IT/BT and S&T, pays up to ₹50 lakh in grants to top-ranked startups. The Karnataka Startup Cell also connects founders to national schemes and DPIIT recognition support. Karnataka remains one of India’s most active state startup ecosystems.

items.title: Maharashtra — MSME Policy 2019 Incentives
items.body: Maharashtra’s MSME Policy offers capital investment subsidies (5–20% on fixed capital, depending on zone and category), electricity duty exemptions, and stamp duty waivers. Micro units in backward regions and businesses owned by women or SC/ST entrepreneurs receive higher subsidy percentages.

items.title: Telangana — T-Hub and WE Hub
items.body: T-Hub is among India’s largest startup incubators and opens access to national and international funding, corporate partnerships, and acceleration programmes. WE Hub focuses on women entrepreneurs with mentoring, market access, and funding facilitation. Both are government-backed and free to apply.

items.title: Rajasthan — i Start Rajasthan
items.body: Rajasthan’s iStart programme offers seed funding of up to ₹5 lakh for registered startups, plus government procurement access, mentoring, and investor introductions. Tourism, handicrafts, IT, and manufacturing startups are especially encouraged to apply.

blocks.text: Eligibility Criteria
Rules differ by programme, but these conditions apply to most central-government MSME grant schemes:

items: Registered as an MSME on the Udyam Registration portal (udyamregistration.gov.in)
Annual turnover inside MSME bands — Micro: up to ₹5 crore, Small: up to ₹50 crore, Medium: up to ₹250 crore
GST registration live, with returns filed for the last 12 months
No NPA (Non-Performing Asset) tag or default with any scheduled commercial bank
Operating in an eligible sector (manufacturing, services, agri-processing — the list changes by scheme)
For DPIIT-funded schemes: a DPIIT Startup Recognition certificate is required
For SC/ST or women-focused schemes: supporting identity or category papers are required

blocks.text: Documents Required
Assembling papers before you start a file saves weeks. This is the standard set most government grant schemes ask for:

items: KYC: Aadhaar card and PAN card (promoter + business entity)
Business registration proof: Udyam Registration certificate, GST certificate, incorporation documents (for Pvt Ltd / LLP)
Financial documents: 2–3 years of ITR (personal + business), CA-certified P&L and balance sheet
Bank statements: 12–24 months of primary business account
Project Report / Detailed Project Report (DPR): Business plan, projected revenue, fund utilisation plan — mandatory for PMEGP and most subsidy schemes
Category certificates (if applicable): SC/ST certificate, women entrepreneur declaration, ex-serviceman certificate
Land or premises proof: Rent agreement or property document for the business location
DPIIT Recognition certificate (for startup-specific schemes like SISFS)

blocks.text: How to Apply
Most central-government grant files are submitted online on scheme-specific portals. The typical path looks like this:

items.title: Identify the Right Schemes
items.body: Match your profile (sector, stage, registration type, founder category) to programmes you actually meet. Do not file for every scheme — concentrate on the 2–3 that fit best. Spreading effort across too many files weakens quality.

items.title: Complete Prerequisite Registrations
items.body: Confirm Udyam Registration and GST are active. For DPIIT-specific schemes, obtain DPIIT Startup Recognition first (startupindia.gov.in). These registrations are free and most take under 30 minutes.

items.title: Prepare Your Documents and Project Report
items.body: Collect KYC, business registration papers, 2–3 years of financials, and bank statements. For PMEGP and subsidy schemes, write a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that sets out the business plan, machinery or equipment to be bought, and projected employment and revenue.

items.title: Register on the Scheme Portal and Submit
items.body: Open an account on the relevant portal (kviconline.gov.in for PMEGP, seedfund.startupindia.gov.in for SISFS, standupmitra.in for Stand-Up India). Complete the online form, upload documents, and submit. Most schemes accept rolling applications — there is no fixed deadline.

items.title: Follow Up with the Nodal Agency
items.body: After filing, a nodal officer (DIC officer for PMEGP, incubator committee for SISFS) reviews the file and may set a physical inspection or presentation. Track status on the portal and answer queries quickly.

items.title: Comply With Post-Sanction Requirements
items.body: Once a grant or subsidy is sanctioned, most schemes ask for utilisation certificates, periodic progress reports, and sometimes bank-account-level tracking of spend. Non-compliance can lead to recovery of sanctioned amounts.

blocks.text: Profitability Breakdown: What to Expect

blocks.text: Union Budget 2026 is a turning point for the Indian economy, built around a clear plan to strengthen Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman unveiled measures meant to speed up growth so Indian MSMEs can compete as global champions. The budget uses a three-part strategy for MSME development: funding support, simpler policy, and market access at home and abroad.

MSMEs already sit at the centre of the economy, adding substantially to jobs, GDP, and exports. The programmes announced in Budget 2026 are expected to open a wave of opportunities that encourage innovation, expansion, and sustainability.
Key Highlights from the Union Budget 2026 for MSMEs
The announcements from Union Budget 2026 with the strongest direct effect on MSMEs are:

items.title: Rs. 10,000 Crore SME Growth Fund
items.body: Among the most important MSME measures in Budget 2026 is the Rs. 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund. It is meant to back growth and innovation by channelling [equity-based investment](/services/startup) into high-potential businesses.

items.title: Self-Reliant India Fund — Rs. 2,000 Crore Top-Up
items.body: The Self-Reliant India Fund (SRI) was launched to back micro-enterprises. In Union Budget 2026, the government proposed a further Rs. 2,000 crore for this fund to support micro-enterprises, especially in manufacturing, through grants and subsidies.

items.title: Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund
items.body: To help MSMEs expand, the government has proposed an Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund. It supplies guarantee cover for infrastructure projects, in a similar way to the [credit guarantee behind collateral-free loans](/scheme/cgtmse) used for large-scale development.

items.title: Duty Benefits for Seafood, Leather, and Textile Exports
items.body: Union Budget 2026 proposes [duty benefits for exports](/blogs/export-promotion-mission), lifting the duty drawback for seafood exports to 3% of FOB value and allowing duty-free imports for leather items such as shoe uppers.

items.title: GST Integration with Ge M and TRe DS
items.body: GST will be linked with GeM (Government e-Marketplace) and TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System). MSMEs should find it easier to win government contracts, and payments will move further onto digital rails.

blocks.text: 10 Benefits Indian MSMEs Get from Union Budget 2026
A closer look at the benefits Indian MSMEs get from this year’s fiscal plan:

items.title: 1\. Easier Access to Funding and Credit
items.body: The Rs. 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund, a larger Self-Reliant India Fund, and the Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund together improve how Indian MSMEs reach credit and capital. The programmes mix equity and debt so that the funding gaps small firms face are easier to close.

items.title: 2\. Tax Relief and Exemptions
items.body: Union Budget 2026 includes tax relief through lower rates and simpler compliance for MSMEs. The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate will fall to 14% from the current 15%, which eases the burden especially in manufacturing — see [what the corporate tax relief means in practice](/blogs/corporate-tax-relief-2026-msme-startup-savings) for a small business.

items.title: 3\. Enhanced Market Access
items.body: Linking GST with GeM and TReDS should widen market access for MSMEs by opening government contracts, business partnerships, and international trade.

items.title: 4\. Increased Competitiveness in Global Markets
items.body: Duty benefits on exports, subsidies, and tax exemptions should improve MSMEs’ price competitiveness abroad, supporting higher exports and more global partnerships.

items.title: 5\. Support for Women Entrepreneurs
items.body: Union Budget 2026 also gives women entrepreneurs extra financial incentives and [funding opportunities for businesses led by women](/scheme), which supports more inclusive growth.

items.title: 6\. Boost to Agri-Tech Startups
items.body: Ongoing attention to agriculture includes backing for agri-tech startups via the [Agri-Sure Fund](/scheme) and the RKVY RAFTAAR scheme, so MSMEs in agri can scale more quickly.

items.title: 7\. Clean Energy Transition Support
items.body: Sustainable and clean energy solutions will get priority funding so MSMEs can move to renewable energy, cut operating costs, and improve sustainability.

items.title: 8\. Digital Transformation Investment
items.body: Large spending on digitization helps MSMEs complete the [startup registration process in India](/services/registration) and take up modern digital tools for operations, marketing, and compliance.

items.title: 9\. Continued Support for CGSS and NIDHI PRAYAS
items.body: Startups can use the [CGSS credit guarantee for startups](/scheme/cgss) and the NIDHI PRAYAS grant, both of which keep receiving support in this budget, so early-stage innovators still have prototype funding.

items.title: 10\. Simplified Compliance and Regulatory Relief
items.body: The budget adds steps that simplify compliance for MSMEs, easing the regulatory load so firms can concentrate on growth instead of paperwork.

blocks.text: Focus Areas for MSME Growth in Union Budget 2026
The government has singled out particular sectors to advance the 'Green India' and 'Digital India' movements:

items: Agri-tech: Ongoing attention to agriculture, with support for agri-tech startups through the Agri-Sure Fund and RKVY RAFTAAR scheme.

Union Budget 2026 is a major shift for Indian MSMEs, bringing substantial financial support, tax relief, and market access. Through targeted programmes such as the SME Growth Fund and the Self-Reliant India Fund, Indian MSMEs are in a position to expand and compete as global champions.

blocks.text: Andhra Pradesh’s small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) have a new opening: the AP-MSME Export Development Convention 2025 has put overseas markets, finance, and digital trade tools within reach of local firms. Day One already produced business projections of ₹174 crore. The convention also sits inside a wider [national export promotion push](/blogs/export-promotion-mission) meant to put more small manufacturers on foreign order books. This article covers the main takeaways and why Andhra Pradesh is positioning itself as a leader in helping MSMEs sell overseas.
A Giant Leap for Andhra Pradesh's MSMEs
Visiting international buyers projected deals worth ₹174 crore on the convention’s first day. That figure is a clear marker of overseas interest in what the state’s MSMEs make and supply.

The convention has also marked Andhra Pradesh as a leading Indian state for MSME growth. It created a space where local firms can innovate, partner, and sell worldwide.

blocks.text: Indian commerce is changing at a fundamental level. Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal, on February 20, 2026, rolled out seven extra interventions under the Export Promotion Mission (EPM), a move aimed at anchoring India more firmly among the world’s leading trading nations.

These additions are more than incremental rules for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) — they function as a pathway into international markets. For founders still mapping out how to raise funds for a startup in India with an overseas push in mind, the Export Promotion Mission is the mechanism that can keep that expansion going.
What is the Export Promotion Mission (EPM)?

Run by the Department of Commerce, the Export Promotion Mission (EPM) is a signature programme whose core aim is to raise the worldwide competitiveness of Indian exporters, with particular attention on MSMEs, startups, and new-generation entrepreneurs.
The programme rests on a 'Twin-Pillar' design:

items: Niryat Protsahan: Built around money-side tools and lending access.
Niryat Disha: Built around the broader trading environment, cargo movement, and regulatory alignment.

blocks.text: 7 New Interventions: Breaking Down the Framework

With Piyush Goyal’s newest declaration, 10 of the 11 interventions planned under the Export Promotion Mission are now live. The fresh set concentrates on online trade, cash availability, and cargo systems.

items.title: 1\. Export Factoring Support
items.body: Lets firms [collect cash promptly against invoices](/blogs/factoring-in-nigeria). Benefit: A 2.75% interest subvention on eligible transactions. Limit: Capped at Rs 50 lakh per MSME annually. Must be processed through RBI or IFSCA-recognized entities.

items.title: 2\. Direct E-Commerce Credit Facility
items.body: Supplies [working capital for e-commerce retail exports](/services/loan). Financial Support: Up to Rs 50 lakh. Security: Offers a 90% guarantee coverage, reducing the risk for lending institutions.

items.title: 3\. Overseas Inventory Credit Facility
items.body: Enables exporters to hold dispatch-ready inventory in major foreign markets. Financial Support: Credit up to Rs 5 crore. Security: A 75% guarantee coverage.

items.title: 4\. TRACE (Trade Regulations, Accreditation & Compliance Enablement)
items.body: Offers money-back support for testing and certification. Reimbursement: 60% for the Positive List and 75% for the Priority Positive List. Annual Ceiling: Up to Rs 25 lakh per IEC (Importer-Exporter Code).

items.title: 5\. FLOW (Facilitating Logistics, Overseas Warehousing & Fulfilment)
items.body: Intended to shrink the gap in logistics expenses. Support: Assistance for overseas warehousing and e-commerce export hubs. Funding: Up to 30% of the approved project cost for a duration of three years.

items.title: 6\. LIFT (Logistics Interventions for Freight & Transport)
items.body: Assists exporters based in districts that have not historically served as export centres. Reimbursement: Up to 30% of eligible freight expenditure. Cap: Rs 20 lakh per IEC annually.

items.title: 7\. INSIGHT (Integrated Support for Trade Intelligence & Facilitation)
items.body: Centres on skill development and market intelligence. Funding: Up to 50% of project cost for private proposals and 100% for government proposals. Focus: Trade intelligence systems and exporter training.

Why These Interventions Matter for MSMEs
The Export Promotion Mission goes beyond handing out subsidies; it constructs a complete architecture for scaling up.

items: Reducing the Cost of Capital: Interest subventions and credit guarantees bring down the rates MSMEs actually pay, putting them on par with [subsidised Mudra credit](/scheme/mudra).
Strengthening Global Competitiveness: Firms can now meet the [certifications required to sell in the EU, USA, and Japan](/services/certificate) without the earlier cost barrier.

Leveraging Free Trade Agreements (FTAs): Several FTAs, among them the India-EU Free Trade Agreement, have already been concluded. The EPM supplies the financial 'muscle' needed to actually use those agreements.

blocks.text: Implementation Partners: A Coordinated Effort
Delivering the Export Promotion Mission requires several arms of government to move in step:

items: Ministry of MSME & Ministry of Finance: Policy and budgetary support.
EXIM Bank: Providing the credit and guarantee frameworks.
Indian Missions Abroad: Acting as the 'on-ground' intelligence for Indian exporters.

blocks.text: Steps to Benefit from the Export Promotion Mission
Use this sequence to tap EPM support for your firm:

items.title: Obtain an IEC
items.body: Confirm that your Importer-Exporter Code is live before you apply under any EPM intervention.

items.body: Check whether you sit on the 'Positive List' that governs TRACE compliance reimbursements.

items.title: Consult Experts
items.body: Our advisory practice is built around making this simpler, supporting you as you draft [applications for government grants](/services/grant) and EPM interventions.

blocks.text: Emerging Technologies and Exports

Minister Goyal underlined that tomorrow’s export growth will sit in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Quantum Computing. The EPM is structured to back startups in these advanced fields so India can ship high-value intellectual property, with backing also available through programmes such as [MeitY Genesis EIR](/services/grant).
Conclusion

Adding these seven interventions to the Export Promotion Mission is a watershed moment for 'Make in India'. By tackling the price of capital, cargo costs, and compliance, the EPM puts smaller firms on more even footing. For an Indian MSME, overseas markets are now a realistic opening rather than a distant idea.

blocks.text: Launching a company or building something new in Gujarat can pay off, particularly when the right finance is available. Funding Support Gujarat is a government programme that channels money and mentoring to startups and innovators in the state. It is designed to back entrepreneurs with grants, subsidies, and other financial help so they can grow and create real impact. If you have never applied before, it is useful to know [what grant funding actually involves](/blogs/how-government-grants-work) before you begin gathering papers.
This guide covers the Funding Support Gujarat Scheme in full — the programme itself, eligibility, priority sectors, benefits, paperwork, and how to apply step by step.
What is the Funding Support Gujarat Program?

Funding Support Gujarat is a Government of Gujarat initiative meant to help startups and innovators in the state turn ideas into products and then scale them. Run through various government agencies, it offers finance, mentoring, and business support so startups can expand and make a mark in their fields.
The scheme mainly backs startups and innovators whose products are ready for the market and can deliver meaningful social impact, and it aims to help them grow inside Gujarat as well as outside it.
Eligibility Criteria for Funding Support Gujarat
Applicants need to satisfy the following conditions to be considered for Funding Support Gujarat:
[Private Limited Company, LLP, or Registered Partnership](/services/registration)
The startup/innovator must be based in Gujarat and have significant operations in the state

headers: The applicant must not own more than 10% in any other company
rows: Startups in ideation, designing, proof-of-concept, productization, or scaling stage are eligible
The founder or co-founder must be an individual who is based in Gujarat

blocks.text: Focus Sectors Supported by Funding Support Gujarat
The programme is aimed at startups building innovative products and solutions in a range of fields:
The scheme supports startups working in all sectors where innovation is the key, such as technology, manufacturing, and more
Startups focused on health technology, telemedicine, healthcare innovations, and MedTech
Solutions aimed at promoting renewable energy, waste management, clean technologies, and environmental protection
Innovations in financial technologies that improve financial inclusion, payments, and lending
Startups leveraging [artificial intelligence and machine learning](/blogs/ai-tools-for-business), and robotics for industry applications
Technologies aimed at improving farming techniques, crop management, and precision agriculture
Benefits of the Funding Support Gujarat
Eligible startups can access a mix of financial and non-financial support under Funding Support Gujarat:
Up to ₹30 Lakhs in grant support for eligible startups
Up to ₹5 Lakhs [additional funding for women-led startups](/scheme)
₹20,000 per month for one year for approved startups; ₹25,000 per month for women-led startups
Up to ₹1 Lakh for skill development and training programs for the startup team
Waiver of virtual incubation fees for approved startups
INR 50 Lakhs to INR 3 Crore in [pre-series A funding](/services/startup) from Gujarat Venture Finance Limited (GVFL)
Additional 1% subsidy on interest rates for MSMEs under the scheme
Documents Required for Funding Support Gujarat Application
When you apply for Funding Support Gujarat, you need to file the papers listed below:
Certificate of Incorporation (COI), MoA, AoA
Proof of registration with KSUM (Kerala Startup Mission)
Bank account details for funding disbursement
Identity proof (e.g., PAN card, Aadhaar card) of the founder(s)
A detailed pitch deck or business plan outlining your product, market opportunity, and [growth strategy](/services/growth)
Profit & Loss Account, Balance Sheet, and fund utilization breakdown
How to Apply for the Funding Support Gujarat
Applying to Funding Support Gujarat follows these steps:

items.title: Step 1: Prepare Documents
items.body: Assemble the full set of papers — incorporation proof, pitch deck, financials, and founder identity documents.

items.title: Step 2: Submit Application
items.body: File the application on the official programme portal and attach every required document.

items.title: Step 3: Evaluation Process
items.body: The programme team reviews the application for innovation, market potential, and whether you meet the eligibility rules.

items.title: Step 4: Shortlisting and Interview
items.body: Applicants who make the shortlist are called for an interview with the selection committee, which then makes the final assessment.

items.title: Step 5: Grant Disbursement and Support
items.body: Startups that are selected receive the grant along with mentoring, incubation, and access to [the GVFL network](/scheme/gvfl).

blocks.text: Is There a Deadline for Applying to the Funding Support Gujarat?
Funding Support Gujarat takes applications on a rolling basis, and specific closing dates are published during the year. Check the official website for current deadlines and open windows.
Conclusion: Why Apply for the Funding Support Gujarat?

For innovators and founders in Gujarat, Funding Support Gujarat is a strong route to finance, mentoring, and business support that can help a startup grow. Grants of up to ₹30 Lakhs, interest subsidies, and incubation assistance give you the tools to take the venture further. If you would rather not handle the process alone, our [funding consultancy in Gujarat](/services/funding) works through eligibility, documentation and submission with you.

items.body: Government bodies or incubators check that documents are genuine, that the project is feasible, that it is innovative, and that it can deliver social or economic impact. Interviews or presentations may be part of the process.

items.title: Approval & Agreement
items.body: Successful applicants sign a grant agreement confirming the money will be spent only on the approved purpose, that reports will be filed on schedule, and that compliance will be kept up.

items.title: Release of Funds
items.body: Money is paid out in stages by direct bank transfer, on a reimbursement basis, against milestones, or as an advance, depending on the scheme.

blocks.text: Why Does the Government Give Grants?

Govt grants exist to back economic development, entrepreneurship, women empowerment, skill building, technology innovation, rural development, education and research, environmental work, and job creation. They generate employment, strengthen industries, and lift communities.
Types of Government Grants in India
India has several kinds of government grants, each aimed at different sectors, needs, and applicant groups:

items.title: Direct Financial Grants
items.body: Cash awards from the government to back particular initiatives. Money is typically earmarked for projects that fit the government’s development priorities. Startup India Seed Fund and NIDHI PRAYAS are examples.

items.title: Subsidy-Based Grants
items.body: These awards cut the cost of specified projects by covering a portion of the spend. The [PMEGP subsidy for new micro-enterprises](/scheme/pmegp) pays a share of project cost in manufacturing and services.

items.title: Reimbursement Grants
items.body: You spend first, then file papers to recover the cost. This model is common in research and development, where project expenses are incurred before the grant is claimed.

items.title: Seed Funding Grants
items.body: Early-stage startups use seed funding grants to build prototypes or proofs of concept. SISFS (Startup India Seed Fund Scheme) can provide up to ₹50 Lakhs.

items.title: Research and Innovation Grants
items.body: Universities, researchers, and startups working on new technologies receive these awards. Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) and DBT grants sit in this group.

items.title: Social Impact Grants
items.body: These awards back [NGOs and social enterprises](/services/registration) active in education, healthcare, environmental conservation, and community development. The National Clean Energy Fund is a well-known example.

items.title: Women Empowerment Grants
items.body: Aimed at women entrepreneurs, NGOs, and organisations working on women’s welfare and gender equality. Mahila Coir Yojana and WEP (Women Entrepreneurship Platform) are leading examples, along with dedicated [grants for women entrepreneurs](/scheme).

items.title: MSME Grants
items.body: Small and medium enterprises can access schemes that support innovation, expansion, and upskilling. The MSME Innovation Fund helps firms grow in manufacturing, services, and technology.

items.title: Educational and Skill Development Grants
items.body: These focus on training, skill building, and higher education. Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) funds vocational training programmes and entrepreneurial support.

items.title: Step 2: Check Eligibility
items.body: Each scheme has tight rules on age, gender, business type, income, location, category (SC/ST/OBC/General), and the purpose of the project.

items.title: Step 3: Prepare Your Documents
items.body: Papers typically include Aadhaar, PAN, [business registration](/services/registration), bank details, a project report, a budget, machinery quotations, a pitch deck (for startups), and NGO registration (for NGOs).

items.body: File through official government portals, incubator portals (for Startup India), the District Industries Centre (DIC), or NGO registration portals.

items.body: Authorities check documents, background, business feasibility, and technical viability. Some schemes also need incubator clearance, video KYC, or a panel interview.

items.title: Step 6: Grant Approval
items.body: After approval you receive a sanction letter, the terms and conditions, and a timeline for the funding.

items.title: Step 7: Fund Release
items.body: Money is paid in phases by bank transfer to the beneficiary, as reimbursement after you invest, or against milestones for startups and R&D.

blocks.text: Top Government Grants in India (Updated 2025)

items.title: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS)
items.body: Offers seed funding of up to ₹50 Lakhs so early-stage startups can develop products, enter markets, and scale. Eligibility: a startup registered under Startup India with an innovative product at seed or ideation stage.

items.title: PMEGP (Prime Minister's Employment Generation Program)
items.body: Pays subsidies of 15–35% of total project cost for micro and small businesses in urban and rural areas. Eligibility: new micro and small enterprises in manufacturing or services.

items.body: Aimed at MSMEs in manufacturing or services, these grants support innovation, product development, and expansion, including machinery buys and market research. Browse the current [innovation and expansion schemes for MSMEs](/scheme) to see which are open.

Helps small businesses grow

blocks.text: Common Myths About Government Grants
Plenty of misunderstandings surround how government grants work. Clearing them up can help you use these programmes well:

items.title: Myth 1: Government grants are free money
items.body: Reality: Grants do not have to be repaid, but you still need a thorough proposal, evidence that the project can work, and ongoing reporting if you want the funding to continue.

items.title: Myth 2: Only big businesses get government funding
items.body: Reality: Small businesses, startups, and even individuals can receive government grants. A large number of schemes are built specifically for MSMEs and startups.

items.title: Myth 3: Government grants are difficult to get
items.body: Reality: Applying can be reasonably straightforward once you know the eligibility rules and guidelines. Planning and organisation raise the odds of a sanction considerably.

items.body: Reality: New firms and startups qualify for several schemes. Startup India, MUDRA, and SISFS are aimed specifically at new businesses.

items.body: Reality: Whether the project is feasible, the quality of the business plan, and your ability to deliver matter as much as how strong the idea is.

items.body: Reality: Most government grants require periodic reports, milestone reviews, and progress updates so authorities can confirm funds are being used correctly.

blocks.text: The India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) — which specialists often label the 'Mother of All Deals' — is a historic shift in how the two sides trade. The completed pact is expected to recast commerce between India and the European Union (EU). For startups, companies, and founders in both places it is a major change, unlocking a combined market of nearly $27 trillion.
Indian founders who have already worked out how to raise funds for a startup in India and now want to go overseas will find this agreement a direct route into Europe.
Why is the India-EU Trade Agreement Called the 'Mother of All Deals'?

The India-EU FTA is a landmark pact arriving at a sensitive moment of global trade disruption and changing geopolitics. It spans two billion people and about 25% of world GDP, giving participants rare access to the largest free-trade zone on the planet.
The 'Mother of All Deals' is also viewed as a strategic response to trade policies from other major powers that had earlier imposed higher tariffs on both India and the EU.

items: $27 Trillion Market: Combined GDP of India and the EU ranks among the largest markets worldwide.
Tariff Reduction: Indian tariffs will fall sharply, easing two-way access into key industries.
Sectoral Focus: Agriculture, clean energy, healthcare, IT, telecom, and manufacturing are among the many sectors that stand to gain from this trade agreement.
Strategic Balance: The pact opens new markets and supports regional economic integration, with innovation and inclusive growth in view.

blocks.text: What Does the India-EU Trade Agreement Cover?
The India-EU Trade Agreement reaches across many industries. The main areas where the two sides have agreed to cut tariffs are:
India will open its automobile market to EU imports, reducing Indian tariffs on luxury cars and [electric vehicles](/blogs/ev-charging-station-business-in-2026-50-lakh-profit-roadmap).
Major tariff reductions for [pharmaceuticals and medical devices](/blogs/how-to-get-drug-manufacturing-license-in-india), and healthcare services.
Collaboration in renewable energy, solar, and wind power.
Agricultural products like seafood, fruits, and vegetables will have better access to EU markets, backed by [agri-business grant support](/scheme) at home.
[Indian textile industries](/services/grant) will benefit from duty reductions when exporting to the EU.
Tariffs will be reduced on machinery and automated systems, supported by [the MSME Act](/blogs/msme-act).
How Will Tariffs Be Reduced for India and the EU?
Under the India-EU Free Trade Agreement, tariffs are expected to fall on nearly 96.6% of EU goods exports to India. Preferential access is built in for core industries:

items: Machinery & Electronics: Tariffs on EU engineering goods entering India will drop sharply.
Steel: India will be able to ship up to 1.6 million tonnes of steel to the EU without tariffs, improving access for heavy industry.
Wines & Spirits: Duties on EU wines will come down from 150% to roughly 20–30%.

blocks.text: What Does the India-EU Trade Deal Mean for Indian Startups?
For Indian startups, the 'Mother of All Deals' creates substantial room to grow:

items.title: Reduced Tariffs on Goods Exports
items.body: Manufacturing and pharmaceutical startups will face a lower cost of entering the EU market.

items.title: Access to EU Funding
items.body: The pact includes better financing provisions, so Indian startups can draw EU investors when they scale globally.

items.title: Tech Collaborations
items.body: The agreement encourages joint work in AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology. Startups can seek European partners as they expand worldwide.

items.title: IPR Support
items.body: Closer alignment of IPR standards makes it safer for startups holding a [Startup India Certificate](/services/startup) to protect patents in Europe.

blocks.text: Impact on Global Business Relations

The pact places India more firmly in global trade. Lower tariffs and simpler access to Europe let Indian firms [diversify their export portfolios](/blogs/export-promotion-mission) and rely less on markets that may levy higher duties.

items: Stronger Economic Relations: India and the EU can deepen their strategic partnership around innovation and technology transfer.
Job Creation: Higher production in manufacturing and agri-tech is expected to generate millions of new jobs.
Counterbalancing Higher Tariffs: While protectionism rises elsewhere, this deal functions as a stabilizer for the world economy.
New Trade Partnerships: Fresh partnerships with European companies are likely, especially in sustainability and social-impact innovation.

blocks.text: Conclusion: A Game Changer for the $27 Trillion Market

The India-EU Free Trade Agreement — the 'Mother of All Deals' — unlocks a wide set of opportunities. By cutting tariffs for India, widening market access, and tightening economic links, the pact casts both regions as major global economic powers.
As India continues its [MSME growth advisory](/services/growth), this FTA supplies the bridge to success abroad. For Indian founders, it is a rare chance to scale and to work with global leaders.

title: Minimum Capital Requirement for LLP in India: A Comprehensive Guide (2026)
excerpt: Understand how much capital an LLP needs in India, how partners contribute funds, what paid-up capital means, and how to launch an LLP without a large outlay — with specialist support if you want it.
imageAlt: Minimum Capital Requirement for LLP in India: A Comprehensive Guide (2026)
takeaways: What is an LLP?
Is There Any Minimum Capital Requirement for an LLP in India?
Can I Register an LLP with ₹1 Capital?

blocks.text: Among the structures Indian founders choose when they launch, the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) stands out for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). People pick it because it offers operational flexibility, limited personal liability, and lighter compliance than alternatives such as a private limited company. A question that surfaces again and again is what the minimum capital requirement for LLP in India actually is.

This article walks through the minimum capital for LLP in India, the minimum capital contribution for LLP in India, and the related rules so you can form your LLP with a clear picture of what is required.
What is an LLP?

A Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) in India sits between a traditional partnership and a limited liability company, borrowing traits from both. Its main advantage is that each partner’s exposure stops at the capital they have agreed to put in, so personal wealth is shielded from the firm’s debts.

The LLP Act, 2008 governs this form. Small firms, professional practices, and startups often prefer it because the structure is adaptable and ongoing compliance is relatively inexpensive. If you are still comparing entity types, our [LLP and company registration service](/services/registration) explains the obligations that come with each option.
Is There Any Minimum Capital Requirement for an LLP in India?
Many people assume that forming an LLP in India requires a fixed minimum capital. In reality, the LLP Act does not set any minimum capital requirement to incorporate an LLP.
Private limited companies, by contrast, have historically needed a minimum paid-up capital of ₹1 lakh. An LLP can be registered with a capital contribution as low as ₹1.

In legal terms, the LLP Act does not impose a minimum capital contribution for LLP in India. Partners themselves decide how much they will put in. What the law does require is that every partner agrees on that amount and that it is written clearly into the LLP Agreement.

items: Starting an LLP does not require a prescribed capital floor.
Partners set the contribution by mutual agreement, with room to choose the amount.

blocks.text: Can I Register an LLP with ₹1 Capital?

You may lawfully incorporate an LLP with ₹1, or with any other small sum the partners settle on. Nothing in the statute blocks an LLP that begins with very little capital. That said, the contribution should still match what the business actually needs at the outset.
A ₹1 figure can get you through registration, but it rarely impresses banks or [investors evaluating your company](/services/startup) down the line.
Does the LLP Act Mandate a Minimum Paid-Up Capital?

Private limited companies must meet a minimum paid-up capital under the Companies Act. LLPs have no equivalent rule under the LLP Act. Partners may contribute in whatever proportions they jointly accept. A founder working alone who wants limited liability without a second partner can also review the [one-person company route](/services/opc).
Paid-up capital of an LLP is simply the total of every partner’s contribution. That total has to appear in the LLP Agreement and be submitted to the Registrar of LLPs.
What is the Effect of Declaring Very Low Capital in an LLP?
Putting a very small capital figure on the LLP can affect how outsiders see the firm and how banks treat it:

items.title: Credibility Issues
items.body: A contribution of ₹1 or ₹5 can make lenders and investors doubt whether the venture is serious and how large its operations really are, particularly when you approach them for money.

items.title: Bank Accounts
items.body: Banks often expect a meaningful capital contribution before they will open a business account or extend credit. An extremely low amount can make it harder to obtain [loans or credit lines](/services/loan).

items.title: Investors
items.body: Outside investors and funders may worry about the firm’s stability and upside if the capital base looks too thin.

blocks.text: Are There Audit Requirements Based on Capital Contribution in an LLP?

Capital contribution does not, by itself, trigger an audit. Under the LLP Act, a statutory audit becomes compulsory when annual turnover goes above ₹40 lakhs or when capital contribution goes above ₹25 lakhs. Meeting either threshold means a chartered accountant must audit the accounts every year.

items: The annual turnover exceeds ₹40 lakhs, or
The capital contribution exceeds ₹25 lakhs.

blocks.text: How to Value Non-Cash Capital Contributions (Assets or Services) in LLP?

If a partner puts in assets or services rather than cash, those contributions need a fair value in the LLP agreement. Assets might be property, machinery, or equipment given to the firm. Services might be the assessed worth of management skill or [intellectual property contributed by a partner](/services/legal), which should be recorded with care.

items.title: Market Value
items.body: Determine what the asset or service would fetch in the market today.

items.title: Professional Appraisal
items.body: Ask a certified valuer or auditor for an independent assessment.

items.title: Depreciated Value
items.body: For physical assets, use the depreciated figure so the value reflects wear and tear to date.

blocks.text: Can Partners Change Their Capital Contribution Later in an LLP?

Partners may revise their contributions whenever they all agree and then update the LLP Agreement — among the [founding documents worth keeping current](/blogs/startup-legal-documents). That flexibility lets people raise or lower their financial stake as the business grows or its needs shift. Revisions can mean adding or reducing capital, altering each partner’s share of the contribution, or moving capital from one partner to another.
Is Stamp Duty on LLP Agreement Dependent on Capital Contribution?

Stamp duty frequently applies to the LLP Agreement, and in some states the charge is tied to the capital contribution. Maharashtra, for example, levies stamp duty according to the total capital stated in the agreement, whereas other states use a flat stamp duty. Confirm the rate that applies in the state where the LLP is registered.
How Does Capital Contribution in LLP Affect Profit Sharing Among Partners?

Unless the LLP Agreement says otherwise, capital contribution sets how profits are divided among partners. The split can track each partner’s contribution, or the partners can write a different arrangement (for instance a 50:50 split). A larger contribution can mean a larger profit share, unless everyone has agreed to something else.
Conclusion: Minimum Capital Requirement for LLP in India

India does not impose a minimum capital requirement for an LLP, yet capital still matters for day-to-day operations and for how the firm is perceived. Partners may put in cash or non-cash assets, provided those inputs are valued properly and recorded.

Contribution also shapes profit-sharing, though the ratio can be rewritten later. Firms that expect to raise loans or outside funding benefit from a credible capital base — something to settle while [planning your funding route](/services/funding), not after a lender flags it.

blocks.text: The Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 — usually called the MSME Act — was brought in by the Government of India as a single legal framework to back the expansion of small and medium firms. In today’s economy, MSMEs are treated as the backbone of India, adding substantially to jobs, GDP, and exports.

The MSME Act 2006 is meant to help small businesses grow by easing access to credit, subsidies, tax exemptions, and other support. Founders who are working out how to raise funds for a startup in India should treat this statute as the starting point of that path.
What is the MSMED Act, 2006?

The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006 was passed to promote the growth, development, and competitiveness of micro, small, and medium enterprises in India, and to deal with related and incidental issues. A notable change under the Act is that medium enterprises were brought within its reach, and service-based businesses were recognised as MSMEs, which widened the sector’s coverage.
Key Features of the MSME Act 2006
The MSME Act treats enterprises as either manufacturing or service businesses and places them in three bands: Micro, Small, and Medium.

items.title: Creating Legal Recognition
items.body: For the first time, micro, small, and medium enterprises received legal recognition inside a single framework.

items.title: Encouraging Innovation
items.body: The statute backs innovative technologies by supporting R&D and technological progress.

items.title: Credit Accessibility
items.body: A core aim of the MSME Act is to make bank credit easier to obtain and to help firms secure [collateral-free business loans](/services/loan).

items.title: Advisory Bodies
items.body: The National Board for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises was set up to look at the factors that affect the sector.

blocks.text: Categories of Enterprises under the MSME Act 2006
The original 2006 definitions were later overhauled. The MSME Act 2020 amendments combined manufacturing and service criteria and introduced turnover as a measure.
The Objective of the MSME Act 2006
The MSME Act 2006 is mainly intended to create conditions in which firms can grow. Its key aims include:

items: Facilitating Development: Putting in place supportive measures, finance, and infrastructure.
Boosting Competitiveness: Offering finance, skill building, and market access through a [structured growth strategy](/services/growth).
Protecting MSMEs: Helping smaller firms compete with large companies through government-backed programmes.
Employment Generation: Using the [PMEGP loan scheme](/scheme/pmegp) and other tools to create jobs in rural and urban areas.

blocks.text: What are the Benefits of the MSME Act 2006?
The MSME Act provides a range of advantages that matter for the survival of small firms:

items.title: Access to Credit and Funding
items.body: The statute helps MSMEs obtain finance at concessional rates. Programmes such as the [Mudra loan scheme](/scheme/mudra) supply essential capital for micro-units.

items.title: Tax Benefits
items.body: MSMEs can claim several tax exemptions. Startups that also hold a Startup India Certificate may take three consecutive years of [income tax exemptions](/contact) under Section 80-IAC.

items.title: Protection Against Payment Delays
items.body: Buyers must pay within 45 days of accepting goods or services. If they do not, they owe the MSME compound interest at three times the bank rate notified by the RBI.

items.title: Collateral-Free Loans
items.body: Through the MSME Act, the [CGTMSE loan scheme](/scheme/cgtmse) offers credit-guarantee cover so founders can borrow without pledging assets.

items.title: Subsidies for Certifications
items.body: MSMEs receive substantial subsidies for patent registration, technology upgrades, and ISO certification.

blocks.text: How Does the MSME Act 2006 Help Startups?
The MSME Act 2006 underpins the startup ecosystem. New ventures get support through:

items: Simplified Registration: Moving to [Udyam Registration](/services/registration) has made the process far smoother.
Grant Support: Access to programmes such as the [NIDHI PRAYAS grant](/services/grant) for prototyping.
Public Procurement: Relief from earnest money deposits (EMD) and prior-turnover conditions in government tenders.
Equity Support: Access to the [equity-linked seed fund](/scheme/seed-fund) and other venture instruments.

blocks.text: MSME Act 2006 for Manufacturing and Service Enterprises
Manufacturing and service firms both sit under the MSME Act’s single framework:

items.title: Manufacturing Enterprises
items.body: Firms that produce or manufacture goods. Size is defined by investment in plant and machinery.

items.title: Service Enterprises
items.body: Firms that supply services, classified by investment in equipment. The group includes IT companies, consultancies, and other service businesses.

blocks.text: Documents Required for MSME Registration

headers: To register and claim the advantages of the MSME Act 2006, firms typically need:
rows: Aadhaar of the applicant and PAN of the enterprise
Certificate of Incorporation or Partnership Deed
ITR and audited balance sheets for the last two years
Account number and IFSC code of the business account
GST registration is mandatory for Udyam registration

Vikas Bharat focuses on helping founders with MSME registration and [DPIIT recognition](/services/startup). Our consultants walk you through MSME Act 2006 compliance so the business can access every government scheme it qualifies for.
Whether the goal is the HP Udgam scheme or a startup spark scheme grant, the team works to keep the paperwork complete and accurate.
Conclusion: Why Register Under the MSME Act 2006?

The MSME Act 2006 is not merely a statute; it functions as a lifeline for India’s small and medium enterprises. Legal protection against delayed payments, access to collateral-free credit, and large tax concessions mean even a small innovator can aim high.
If you are launching a firm or expanding one you already run, registration under the MSME Act is among the most useful steps you can take. It opens the door to government grants and loans.

blocks.text: Founders and owners looking for funding without security are in good company. MSMEs, startups, retailers, manufacturers, and service firms often turn to unsecured business funding when they have nothing to mortgage — or when they would rather not put personal or business property at risk.

A without security business loan — also called an unsecured business loan or a collateral-free business loan — is credit from a bank, NBFC, or other financier that does not require any asset to be pledged.
What is an Unsecured Business Loan?
With an unsecured business loan, money is released without the borrower offering collateral such as property, machinery, fixed deposits, gold, or inventory.

items: Collateral is not asked for
The lender judges the borrower on financial strength
Ticket sizes tend to be moderate
Interest sits above what secured loans charge
Sanction and payout are quicker
A fit for working capital and other short-term uses

blocks.text: Why Businesses Choose No Security Business Loans

Firms pick collateral-free credit when they want to keep assets unencumbered, when they need a fast sanction, when they are still early in their growth, or when they only need a modest working-capital line. Even mature companies tap unsecured loans for short-term liquidity, buying inventory, meeting seasonal peaks, or expanding.

items: They prefer not to put assets at risk
They want a quick sanction
They are still in an early growth phase
They only need a smaller working-capital sum
The business is service-led and holds few assets
They want borrowing terms that stay flexible

blocks.text: Key Features of an Unsecured Business Loan
The main traits of unsecured business loans, in brief:
₹50,000 to ₹50,00,000 (varies by profile)
Working capital, marketing, payroll, stock purchase, expansion
Who Can Apply for an Unsecured Business Loan? (Eligibility)
Lenders look at financial strength rather than collateral. Typical filters are:

items: Business Vintage: Typically 2–3 years of continuous operations
Turnover: Minimum ₹10–30 lakhs annual turnover (varies by lender)
Credit Score: CIBIL Score 700+ preferred
Cash Flow: Healthy bank statement with consistent credits
IT Returns: Minimum 1–2 years filed
Current Loan Obligations: Low outstanding debts
Business Registration: Proprietors, partnerships, LLPs, Pvt Ltd companies, MSMEs

blocks.text: What Are the Types of Unsecured Business Funding?
Several unsecured products exist, each matching a different business need:

items.title: Business Term Loans (Unsecured)
items.body: A conventional facility with a fixed tenor (1–5 years), repayment through EMIs, and a one-time disbursement. Used for expansion, buying equipment, renovation, and marketing.

items.title: Business Overdraft (Unsecured / Dropline OD)
items.body: A revolving limit sitting on a current account. Interest applies only to what you draw. A dropline OD shrinks the limit each month. Useful when cash flow swings or when inventory is bought seasonally.

items.title: CGTMSE Collateral-Free Loan
items.body: A [government-backed guarantee scheme for MSMEs](/scheme/cgtmse). Borrowing can go up to ₹2 crore with no collateral. The government supplies the guarantee cover. Open to both new and existing MSMEs.

items.title: Unsecured Working Capital Loan
items.body: Short-tenor money for salaries, stock, vendor bills, and modest upgrades.

items.title: Invoice-Based Unsecured Loans
items.body: Advances against invoices issued to corporates. A match for firms with solid B2B receivables — see how [funding against corporate receivables](/blogs/factoring-in-nigeria) is priced and who bears collection risk.

blocks.text: How Can I Get a Business Loan Without Giving Any Security?
A straightforward sequence to obtain an unsecured business loan:

items.title: Step 1: Assess Your Eligibility
items.body: Check your CIBIL score, years in business, turnover, and banking record so you know where you stand on eligibility.

items.title: Step 2: Collect Required Documents
items.body: Assemble KYC, proof of the business, bank statements, ITRs, and statements for any loans already on the books.

items.title: Step 3: Identify Suitable Lenders
items.body: Weigh banks, NBFCs, and fintech lenders on rates, ticket size, and who they will finance.

items.title: Step 4: Apply Online or Through Consultant
items.body: File the application yourself online, or work with a consultancy such as Vikas Bharat for [professional file preparation](/services/funding).

items.title: Step 5: Financial Evaluation
items.body: The lender reviews your numbers, credit score, and the health of the business before deciding.

items.title: Step 6: Approval & Disbursement
items.body: Once sanctioned, the money is credited to the business account in 24 hours to 7 days.

blocks.text: Which Banks or NBFCs Offer Unsecured Business Loans?
Banks that commonly extend unsecured business loans include HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Axis Bank, IDFC First Bank, SBI (on a selective basis), and IndusInd Bank.

Among NBFCs, names include Bajaj Finserv, Tata Capital, Lendingkart, NeoGrowth, FlexiLoans, Indifi, and InCred. When bank turnaround is the bottleneck, [NBFC financing options](/services/nbfc) typically move quicker, though at a higher rate.
Under CGTMSE, most banks will give MSMEs collateral-free loans backed by a government guarantee.
Documents Required for a Without Security Business Loan

headers: Paperwork usually expected for a collateral-free business loan:
rows: GST certificate, [MSME registration](/services/registration), Shop Act, Partnership Deed

blocks.text: Interest Rates for Collateral-Free Business Loans

The rate you are offered depends on CIBIL score, turnover, banking behaviour, years in business, and the amount requested. Typical pricing sits between 11% and 28% per annum. Fintech lenders often price higher while sanctioning faster.
Can Startups Get a Business Loan Without Collateral?
Startups can access unsecured credit, though the bar is higher. Banks generally want 12+ months of operations and healthy cash flow.

items: CGTMSE loans
[Stand-up India Scheme](/scheme/standup)
Unsecured startup loans from NBFCs
Invoice financing
Business credit cards
Venture debt (for funded startups)

blocks.text: Maximum Loan Amount Available Without Security
How much you can borrow without security tracks financial health and the business profile:

items: For MSMEs: ₹2 lakh – ₹50 lakh
For Larger SMEs: ₹50 lakh – ₹2 crore (rare and profile-based) — see what [larger ticket funding](/blogs/50-lakh-business-loan-2026-secure-high-value-funding) requires
Under CGTMSE: Up to ₹2 crore collateral-free

blocks.text: How Credit Score Affects an Unsecured Business Loan

CIBIL score is the single largest factor in unsecured-loan decisions. A strong score usually brings a lower rate, a larger sanction, and a quicker yes — and it helps to know [which score lenders pull](/blogs/msme-loan-eligibility-2026-commercial-cibil-vs-consumer-cibil), because the firm’s report and the promoter’s report are assessed separately.
Advantages and Disadvantages of No Security Business Loan
A side-by-side look at the strengths and drawbacks of unsecured business loans:
No collateral required — no risk to personal or business assets
Higher interest rates compared to secured loans
Lower loan amounts sanctioned due to higher risk for lenders
Ideal for businesses without fixed assets (service-based, startups, traders)
Shorter repayment tenure (usually 1–5 years)
Flexible usage: working capital, marketing, inventory, payroll
Stricter eligibility criteria (CIBIL score, turnover, banking history)
Simple documentation and minimal paperwork
May be difficult for new businesses with weak financials
Higher chances of rejection if banking behaviour is inconsistent
No need for asset valuation or legal verification
Penalties may be higher in case of late EMI payment
Who Should Apply for an Unsecured Loan?
These facilities suit firms that need money quickly and do not want to mortgage assets:

items: Retailers
Traders

Wholesalers
Restaurants

Manufacturers
Startups needing small working capital

blocks.text: Conclusion: Is a Without Security Business Loan Right for You?

An unsecured business loan is a practical option for MSMEs and startups that need money quickly and have no assets to pledge. Whether the need is working capital, inventory, expansion, or an emergency — unsecured credit can arrive fast and with flexible use.

Sanction, however, rests entirely on how clearly your financials, credit score, and papers are presented. For a stronger chance of approval, a complete file and [the right lender selection](/services/loan) matter a great deal.
